clue.text: "The road was a ribbon of — " (Noyes)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing word completes a line of Alfred Noyes's poem The Highwayman

explanation.walkthrough: The line runs 'The road was a ribbon of moonlight over the purple moor', from Noyes's ballad The Highwayman; the solver simply supplies the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation itself is the definition: the word that fills the gap in the famous line of verse.

clue.text: Many a river, type of rat

parts.note: M, the Roman numeral for a thousand, stands for many
the Usk is a river in South Wales

explanation.surface: Lots of rivers hold a kind of rodent.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a type of rat: the muskrat.
explanation.definitionFit: The muskrat is a North American water rodent named for its scent.

clue.text: At the side of the stage, wine (a French type) is timely

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for an adjective meaning well-timed

parts.words: At the side of the stage
parts.note: OP, opposite prompt, is the side of the stage away from the prompter
port is a fortified wine
une is French for a

explanation.surface: Offstage in the wings, a French-style wine arrives at just the right moment.
explanation.walkthrough: OP (opposite prompt) is theatre jargon for a side of the stage; 'type' just tells you the French word is a type of 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: Opportune means well-timed or coming at a convenient moment.

clue.text: King at city-gate is depressed in Shropshire

definitions.note: a location phrase standing for a place found there

parts.note: the legendary King Lud gave his name to Ludgate, a gate of the City of London
low means depressed

explanation.surface: A monarch at the town's entrance feels down in an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: Ludgate was a gate in London's city wall, named after legendary King Lud; Shropshire is an English county on the Welsh border.
explanation.definitionFit: Ludlow is a market town in Shropshire, England.

clue.text: One who's departed

parts.note: someone who has died or left for good, in casual speech

explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a person who is dead or past saving.

clue.text: Jabberwocky sort of veto

definitions.note: a creature from Lewis Carroll's nonsense poem

indicators.note: sort of tells us to sort or rearrange the letters of the word given

explanation.surface: A kind of ban expressed in nonsense language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges VETO; the 'slithy toves' gyre and gimble in Lewis Carroll's poem Jabberwocky.
explanation.definitionFit: A badger-lizard-corkscrew creature invented in Carroll's poem.

clue.text: Western home of a right Charlie perhaps

definitions.text: Western home of a right Charlie perhaps

parts.words: Western home of a right Charlie perhaps
parts.note: a Western film setting: the cowboy's spread where a fellow like Charlie (a 'right Charlie' being a fool) might live

explanation.walkthrough: 'A right Charlie' is British slang for a fool, which pulls the reader away from the plain picture of a cattle spread in a cowboy film.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Western genre the hero's home is typically a large cattle farm of this kind.

clue.text: Men, in stripes turning up in this unit

indicators.note: in means the soldiers go inside the other piece
in a down clue turning up means reading the word from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: a tiger is the striped big cat, so stripes stand for it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Soldiers wearing stripes rise up within their own company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' reverses TIGER to REGIT, and 'in' puts MEN inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A regiment is a permanent unit of an army.

clue.text: Henrietta, the Shrimp Girl ?

parts.note: a short form of the name Henrietta, read as a girl who catches shrimps with a net

explanation.walkthrough: Hogarth painted 'The Shrimp Girl'; here the girl is a pet form of Henrietta whose name begins with the mesh used to catch shrimps.
explanation.definitionFit: A pet form of Henrietta, punning on the net a shrimper uses.

clue.text: Formerly this was the spot to get a warning

parts.note: here means at this spot
taken as written
fore is the golfer's shout of warning

explanation.surface: A place once marked by a caution sign.
explanation.walkthrough: FORE is what a golfer shouts to warn people in the line of a shot.
explanation.definitionFit: Heretofore means until now, previously.

clue.text: Port with a soft centre is savoury

indicators.note: having something as its centre means that letter goes into the middle of the port's name

parts.note: Port Said is the Egyptian port at the Suez Canal, so 'Port' gives its second word
p (piano) is the musical abbreviation for soft

explanation.surface: A harbour town with a gentle heart turns out to be tasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with a soft centre' puts P inside SAID, from Port Said in Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapid is a formal word for having a pleasant, strong flavour, so savoury or tasty.

clue.text: Henry as travel guide ?

parts.note: the Portuguese prince Henry sponsored voyages of discovery and is known by a title meaning one who steers or guides a journey

explanation.walkthrough: Prince Henry of Portugal (1394-1460) is remembered by a seafaring epithet; a travel guide who plots a course earns the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: One who plots the route of a ship or plane guides the travel, and Prince Henry bore that title.

clue.text: Our army is uncommonly well equipped here

indicators.note: uncommonly suggests the letters of the two words are arranged in an unusual way

explanation.surface: A remark that our soldiers are unusually well kitted out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncommonly' asks for the letters of OUR ARMY to be rearranged; the definition plays on the place where weapons are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: An arsenal or store of weapons is the place where an army is equipped.

clue.text: One law-maker has the skill to communicate

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
an MP, Member of Parliament, makes laws
art is skill, as in the art of persuasion

explanation.surface: A lone legislator has a talent for getting a message across.
explanation.walkthrough: MP stands for Member of Parliament, a British law-maker.
explanation.definitionFit: To impart news is to pass it on or convey it to someone.

clue.text: Bob, the embezzler, is one to take risks

parts.note: bob was slang for a shilling, abbreviated s
a peculator embezzles public money

explanation.surface: Bob the fraudster is a gambler by nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a name, but it is old British slang for a shilling, written s.
explanation.definitionFit: A speculator invests where there is risk in hope of large gains.

clue.text: No interment for this along with the good

definitions.text: No interment for this along with the good

parts.words: No interment for this along with the good
parts.note: Mark Antony says wickedness lives after men while the good is interred with their bones

explanation.walkthrough: From Julius Caesar: 'The evil that men do lives after them; The good is oft interred with their bones.'
explanation.definitionFit: The wrongdoing Antony says outlives a man, unlike his virtues.

clue.text: Fruit for a corner boy

parts.note: the nursery rhyme boy Little Jack Horner sat in a corner and pulled a fruit out of his Christmas pie

explanation.walkthrough: 'Corner boy' sounds like a street loiterer, but it is Little Jack Horner, who 'sat in the corner' and 'put in his thumb and pulled out' this fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The stone fruit Jack Horner pulled from his pie in the rhyme.

clue.text: Understanding of the devil ?

parts.note: under-standing read literally means what one stands on, the feet, and the devil is pictured with split goat's feet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Understanding' looks like comprehension, but read as 'under-standing' it means the feet; the devil traditionally has a divided hoof.
explanation.definitionFit: A split hoof like a goat's is the traditional mark of the devil, the thing he stands on.

clue.text: Funny king !

definitions.meaning: Edward ..., writer of comic nonsense verse
Shakespeare's tragic old monarch of Britain

explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear wrote humorous limericks; King Lear is Shakespeare's tragic ruler.

clue.text: Children make a right-hand leap

parts.note: the off side is the right-hand side, as of a horse or vehicle
a spring is a leap

explanation.surface: Kids taking a jump to the right.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'off side' of a horse or vehicle is the right-hand side in British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Offspring are a person's children or descendants.

clue.text: The prickly Colonel's taciturnity

parts.note: a touchy military officer's habit of keeping quiet, his periods of saying nothing

explanation.definitionFit: Taciturn people keep their mouths shut, and their quiet spells are what this word names.

clue.text: On tick ? Can do. Good show!

definitions.note: an exclamation of praise standing for an adjective meaning deserving praise

parts.note: to buy on tick is to buy on credit
someone who can do something is able

explanation.surface: Buying on the never-never? No problem. Well done!
explanation.walkthrough: 'On tick' is British slang for buying on credit; the definition 'Good show!' stands for a performance worth praising.
explanation.definitionFit: A creditable performance is a praiseworthy one, the kind greeted with 'good show'.

clue.text: Fliers take a turn in the distance

indicators.note: taking a turn means the airmen's abbreviation is read the other way round

parts.note: the RAF, Royal Air Force, are fliers

explanation.surface: Pilots go up one at a time, far off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' reverses RAF to give FAR, placed after A.
explanation.definitionFit: Something far off or a long way away is said to be seen from afar.

clue.text: Equip for flight

parts.note: to provide a young bird with feathers, or an arrow with its vanes

explanation.definitionFit: To give feathers to a chick or an arrow, readying it to fly.

clue.text: "Drink, puppy, drink" if in a flap

parts.note: to lap is to drink as a dog does
a puppy is a pet

explanation.surface: The title of an old hunting song, sung by someone in a state of panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink, Puppy, Drink' is a Victorian hunting song by Whyte-Melville; the first two words give LAP and PET, and the repeated 'drink' only completes the quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: A lappet is a small flap or fold, of a garment, headdress or flesh.

clue.text: He awarded and won the beauty prize

definitions.text: He awarded and won the beauty prize

parts.words: He awarded and won the beauty prize
parts.note: the Trojan prince judged three goddesses, gave the apple to Aphrodite and won Helen as reward

explanation.walkthrough: In the Judgement of Paris the Trojan prince gave the golden apple to Aphrodite, who rewarded him with Helen, the most beautiful woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The Trojan prince who judged a divine beauty contest and gained Helen of Troy.

clue.text: Contemporary birds get round their work in lumps

indicators.note: the girls surround, so the other piece goes inside

parts.note: dolls was the current slang of the day for girls, also called birds
op, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: Modern young women get through their tasks in heaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Birds' and 'dolls' are both slang for young women, 'contemporary' flagging the slang of the time; 'get round' puts OP (opus) inside DOLLS.
explanation.definitionFit: Dollops are shapeless lumps or blobs of something soft, like food.

clue.text: For a date among the sands ?

definitions.text: For a date among the sands ?

parts.words: For a date among the sands ?
parts.note: a date is the palm fruit, which grows in a fertile watered spot in the desert, not a meeting

explanation.walkthrough: 'Date' suggests a romantic meeting, but it is the fruit of the palm growing at a desert watering place.
explanation.definitionFit: A fertile watered spot in a desert where date palms grow.

clue.text: Whence that heavenly music?

parts.note: the stringed instrument angels are pictured playing in heaven

explanation.definitionFit: Angels are traditionally shown playing this stringed instrument.

clue.text: One way to look for a lord

definitions.meaning: to gaze closely or with difficulty
a nobleman in the House of Lords

explanation.definitionFit: To squint closely at something; and a noble of the realm.

clue.text: Renegades issue orders for wardrobe economies

definitions.meaning: to command that garments be reversed to make them last longer

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is an imperative: telling someone to turn their coats inside out, a thrifty wartime way to renew clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Traitors switch allegiance as though reversing a jacket; and a thrifty instruction to reverse jackets reads the same.

clue.text: A long shot of course

parts.note: on a golf course, the long stroke played from the tee

explanation.walkthrough: 'A long shot' suggests an unlikely chance, but the course is a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf the long opening stroke from the tee with a wooden club bears this name.

clue.text: Flowers in watering-cans

definitions.meaning: blooms of a thorny garden shrub
the perforated spouts that sprinkle water from a can

explanation.definitionFit: The garden blooms and the sprinkler heads on a watering-can share the name.

clue.text: Well-trained, this pigeon ?

parts.note: well-trained read as much travelled on trains, and an extinct American pigeon whose name means a traveller

explanation.walkthrough: 'Well-trained' looks like obedient, but it means someone often on a train; the extinct American bird shares the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A traveller carried in a vehicle, and the name of an extinct North American pigeon.
